items.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: And part of that work was inspired by Duke Ellington’s “Black, Brown and Beige”

ctx.x: No actually I started piano at the age of 19. And I don’t like to — I’m only providing a context. Because I wasn’t a political activist. It was more like okay here I am in Palo Alto, the white suburbs, and all I see is my block and Leave it to Beaver. This is the reality. Whereas there is all kinds of things that are going around outside my neighborhood. I mean there’s East Palo Alto, an African-American area, and then there’s what’s happening in the world with the Vietnam War and what the United States empire

is doing to other countries. But what was to me a turning point was when my cousin, who is currently an art professor and a friend of mine who is a drummer, introduced to me the music of John Coltrane. And even though I was not politically sophisticated or musically sophisticated at that time, I was only 17 or 18 years old, I was able to see how that music was connected — when I say — see I felt that music was connected with Malcolm X and later on I discovered that Malcolm X and that whole tradition of Harlem…

he served in sort of a mentor role. And so I was exposed to like “Black, Brown and Beige,” and a tone parallel to Harlem. And so I began to connect how music was part of life. And so I would say like my music is like an expression of my life. But as an American it means that I’m exposed to a diversity of influences and a younger generation of kids, through Internet, and they have access to a lot of opportunities.

items.title: Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2013
items.q: I’m inspired by Duke Ellington, who was composing music on his deathbed.

ctx.x: He was very noble. I remember when we performed Duke Ellington’s “Come Sunday” I could see the humble and humility. And I mean he was a real warrior and you know, some of the works I pay tribute some of the great artists, like Paul Robeson and Mei Manfang. You know I’m trying to respect those artists who’ve become forgotten. Or like I would say one day American — or one day great American artists and one day alien, with a persecution, and the unofficial ban on Paul Robeson’s life during the McCarthy period of the…

undemocratic. So anyway there’s so much that I’ve learned from Max Roach, and it helped validate the direction of where I’m going and who I am. So it’s taken me years to reflect. And also I had to realize, or learn to realize, because of lot of us, like our heroes when we’re young, that I had a friendship but also a friendship with someone who — you know when you think about heroes there’s this immortality and they’re perfect. But we all have problems. And one of them was deteriorating health. But what inspired…

I wanted to ask you about your composition and the topics and the song titles. Most of your work looks to be allegorical or story driven, historical driven. Have you ever — I’m trying to figure out how to ask this — have you ever had music that comes to you that doesn’t have a specific intent?
